definition: The Wi-Fi Alliance's brand name for wireless local area networks built on the IEEE 802.11 standards. Devices share radio channels in unlicensed bands such as 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.
example: A laptop and a phone on the same home network both talk to one Wi-Fi access point over the same 5 GHz channel.

definition: The IEEE family of standards that defines how wireless LANs work at the physical and MAC layers. Each amendment gets letters (802.11n, 802.11ax, 802.11be), which the Wi-Fi Alliance markets as Wi-Fi 4, 6, 7 and so on.

aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a professional body that publishes engineering standards, including Ethernet (802.3) and Wi-Fi (802.11).
The industry group that owns the Wi-Fi trademark, certifies products for interoperability and, since 2018, names 802.11 generations with numbers such as Wi-Fi 6.
The Wi-Fi Alliance name for 802.11n (2009). It introduced MIMO with multiple spatial streams, 40 MHz channels and frame aggregation, on both 2.4 and 5 GHz.
The Wi-Fi Alliance name for 802.11ac (2013), a 5 GHz-only generation that added 80 and 160 MHz channels, 256-QAM and downlink multi-user MIMO.
The Wi-Fi Alliance name for 802.11ax, certified from 2019. It added OFDMA, 1024-QAM, uplink multi-user MIMO and Target Wake Time, aimed at efficiency in busy networks.
Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) extended into the 6 GHz band where regulators allow it. The protocol is the same; the extra spectrum is the difference.
The Wi-Fi Alliance name for 802.11be, certified from January 2024. It adds 320 MHz channels in 6 GHz, 4096-QAM and Multi-Link Operation.

The unlicensed radio band around 2.400–2.4835 GHz used by older and current Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, microwave ovens and many other devices. It has room for only about three non-overlapping 20 MHz Wi-Fi channels (1, 6 and 11), or four where channels 1–13 are allowed.
The set of Wi-Fi channels between roughly 5.15 and 5.85 GHz. It offers many more 20 MHz channels than 2.4 GHz, enough for several 80 MHz channels, but some channels require DFS radar checks.
Spectrum from about 5.925 to 7.125 GHz opened to Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 in many countries, subject to national power and indoor/outdoor rules. Older 2.4/5 GHz-only clients cannot use it.
The unit of frequency: one cycle per second. Radio channel widths and carrier frequencies are measured in hertz.
example: A 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel spans 20 million hertz of spectrum.

definition: One thousand hertz. Cellular subcarrier spacings are quoted in kilohertz, e.g. 15 kHz for LTE.
One million hertz. Wi-Fi channel widths (20, 40, 80, 160, 320 MHz) and channel centre frequencies are given in megahertz.
One billion (10^9) hertz. Wi-Fi bands are named by their approximate frequency in gigahertz: 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.

Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing: splitting a channel into many narrow, closely spaced subcarriers that each carry part of the data at once. Wi-Fi (since 802.11a/g), LTE and 5G NR all use it because it copes well with echoes.

Orthogonal frequency-division multiple access: OFDM in which groups of subcarriers are assigned to different users in the same transmission. Wi-Fi 6 calls the groups resource units; LTE and NR call them resource blocks.
example: A Wi-Fi 6 AP can send small packets to nine clients in one 20 MHz transmission by giving each a slice of the subcarriers.

definition: One of the many narrow carrier frequencies inside an OFDM channel. Each subcarrier carries its own stream of modulated symbols; a Wi-Fi 6 80 MHz channel has 980 data subcarriers.

Multiple-input multiple-output: using several antennas at each end so a radio can send independent data streams (spatial streams) on the same frequency at the same time, or make one stream more robust.
Multi-user MIMO: an access point uses its antennas to send different spatial streams to several clients at once. Wi-Fi 5 supports it on the downlink; Wi-Fi 6 adds the uplink.
An independent data stream sent simultaneously on the same channel using MIMO. Each stream adds roughly one stream's worth of rate if the radio channel and both devices support it.
example: A phone with two spatial streams at 600 Mbit/s each has a 1,200 Mbit/s PHY rate.

definition: Quadrature amplitude modulation: encoding bits by choosing one of M combinations of amplitude and phase for each symbol. More points (higher M) carry more bits per symbol (log base 2 of M) but need a cleaner signal to tell apart.
example: 1024-QAM has 1,024 points, so each symbol carries 10 bits; 4096-QAM carries 12.

definition: The set of amplitude-and-phase points a QAM signal can choose from, usually drawn as a grid. Denser constellations put points closer together, so less noise is needed to cause a wrong decision.
One unit of a modulated radio signal, held for a fixed time, that represents a group of bits. In Wi-Fi 6 one OFDM symbol lasts 12.8 µs plus a guard interval.
Binary phase-shift keying: the simplest modulation, sending one bit per symbol by flipping the carrier's phase. Wi-Fi uses it at MCS 0 because it survives very weak signals.
In Wi-Fi 6 OFDMA, a group of subcarriers within a channel assigned to one client for a transmission. Small resource units let an AP serve several clients' small packets at once.
A Wi-Fi 6 feature in which a device and its access point agree when the device will next wake to send or receive, so its radio can sleep in between and save battery.
A Wi-Fi 7 feature that lets one device associate with an access point over links in more than one band (e.g. 5 and 6 GHz) and use them together or switch between them, depending on mode and hardware.
The Internet of Things: small connected devices such as sensors, plugs and cameras, often battery-powered and sending little data.
The UK's communications regulator, which among other things decides which radio spectrum Wi-Fi and mobile networks may use and on what terms.
Traffic or a link going upstream. In radio, the direction from the device (phone) to the base station or access point; in a data-centre fabric, the links from a leaf switch up to the spines.
Traffic or a link going downstream. In radio, the direction from the base station or access point to the device; in a data centre, a switch's links towards servers.

aliases: carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance
definition: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance: the Wi-Fi rule of listening before transmitting and waiting a random backoff, so that collisions are made unlikely rather than detected. A missing ACK is taken as a sign of failure.

aliases: carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection
definition: Carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection: the classic shared-Ethernet rule of listening before sending and, if a collision is detected while sending, stopping, sending a jam signal and backing off. Switched full-duplex Ethernet no longer needs it.
The dominant family of wired LAN technologies (IEEE 802.3). Modern switched Ethernet gives each device its own full-duplex link to a switch, so devices do not share the medium.
Two or more transmissions overlapping on a shared medium so that a receiver cannot decode either. In Wi-Fi the collision matters at the receiver, which the senders may not be able to hear.
A short signal a shared-Ethernet station sends after detecting a collision, so every station notices it. Wi-Fi never sends one, because it cannot detect collisions.
Listening to the medium before transmitting to check whether another station is already sending. It only works for stations that can hear each other.

Wi-Fi's second way of knowing the channel is busy: stations read the Duration field of frames they overhear and stay quiet for that long, tracked in their NAV, even if they cannot sense the later transmissions.
Network allocation vector: a countdown timer each Wi-Fi station keeps, set from the Duration field of overheard frames. While it is non-zero the station treats the channel as busy.
Waiting a random amount of time before (re)transmitting, so that stations that all wanted to send at once spread out. Exponential backoff widens the random range after each failure.
example: A Wi-Fi station with a contention window of 15 waits 0–15 slots of 9 µs; after a failure, 0–31 slots.

definition: The range, in slots, from which a Wi-Fi station draws its random backoff: 0 to CW. It starts small (15 for 5 GHz best-effort DCF) and roughly doubles after each failed attempt up to a cap such as 1023.
The basic time unit Wi-Fi backoff is counted in: 9 µs for 5 GHz OFDM. Each backoff count is one slot of idle channel.
Distributed Coordination Function: the basic 802.11 contention method, in which each station uses carrier sense, DIFS and random backoff to decide for itself when to transmit.

Enhanced Distributed Channel Access: the QoS version of DCF. Traffic is sorted into access categories (voice, video, best effort, background), each with its own wait and contention-window settings, so voice tends to get on air first.
One of the four EDCA traffic classes in Wi-Fi (voice, video, best effort, background). Each has its own interframe wait and contention-window values.
DCF interframe space: the idle gap a station must see before it may start its backoff countdown. It equals SIFS plus two slots, 34 µs on 5 GHz OFDM.
Short interframe space: the shortest Wi-Fi gap, used before an immediate reply such as an ACK or CTS (16 µs on 5 GHz OFDM). Being shorter than DIFS gives these replies priority.
Acknowledgement: a message confirming that data arrived. In Wi-Fi the receiver sends a short ACK frame after SIFS; in TCP, ACKs report which bytes have been received.
A Wi-Fi acknowledgement that confirms many aggregated frames at once with a bitmap, instead of one ACK per frame.
Sending to exactly one destination. In Wi-Fi, unicast frames are acknowledged; broadcast and multicast frames are not.
Sending one packet to a group of receivers at once. Wi-Fi sends multicast and broadcast frames without per-frame acknowledgement.
Quality of service: treating some traffic preferentially (lower delay, priority, guaranteed share) rather than all packets alike.
Two stations that cannot hear each other but can both reach the same receiver. Carrier sense cannot stop them transmitting at once, so their frames collide at the receiver.
example: A laptop and a scanner at opposite ends of a warehouse both reach the central AP but sense an idle channel and talk over each other.

definition: A station that overhears a nearby transmission and defers, even though its own transmission would not have disturbed the intended receiver. It wastes airtime in dense networks.
Request To Send: a short Wi-Fi frame asking the receiver to reserve the channel, carrying how long the coming exchange will last.
Clear To Send: the receiver's short reply to an RTS, repeating the reservation time so every station near the receiver, including hidden ones, sets its NAV and stays quiet.
The Request To Send / Clear To Send handshake that reserves the channel before a data frame, mainly to protect long frames from hidden-terminal collisions. It costs two extra frames per exchange.
A frame size above which a Wi-Fi device uses RTS/CTS protection before sending; smaller frames go without it. Defaults are device-specific.
The Wi-Fi base station that clients connect to. It bridges the wireless network to a wired one (or to other APs) and coordinates its channel.
When two radio signals collide, a receiver can sometimes still decode the much stronger one. It lets some frames survive collisions.
The choice of which radio channel, and how wide, each access point uses, so neighbouring APs interfere as little as possible. Wider channels carry more data but leave fewer separate channels.
Interference from other transmitters on the same channel. Wi-Fi stations that can decode each other share the channel by contention, which costs airtime but is coordinated.
Interference from a transmitter on an overlapping or neighbouring channel. Its energy can corrupt frames without being decodable, so the networks cannot coordinate.
The regulatory or standard limit on how much power a transmitter may leak outside its channel. It determines how much neighbouring channels interfere.
The country or region whose radio rules apply: which channels, power levels and indoor/outdoor uses are permitted. A Wi-Fi device must be set to the correct one.

Treating the channel as busy because enough radio energy is present, even if no Wi-Fi frame can be decoded from it. Its threshold (about −62 dBm for 20 MHz) is much higher than the roughly −82 dBm at which a decodable Wi-Fi preamble marks the channel busy.
Dynamic Frequency Selection: rules for 5 GHz channels shared with radar. An AP must listen for radar before using them and leave the channel if it detects any, which can cause sudden channel changes.

The weakening of a radio signal between two ideal antennas with nothing in between, as the energy spreads out. It grows with the square of distance and of frequency: about 6 dB more for each doubling of either.
example: Over 10 m the loss is about 60 dB at 2.4 GHz and 67 dB at 5.5 GHz.

definition: How much an antenna concentrates power in its best direction compared with an ideal isotropic antenna that radiates equally in all directions, usually in dBi.
The weakest signal a receiver can still decode at a given data rate. Higher rates need stronger signals.
A short-range wireless standard for devices such as headphones and keyboards. It shares the 2.4 GHz band with Wi-Fi.
The physical layer: the part of a network standard that turns bits into signals on the wire or radio (modulation, coding, timing).

The raw bit rate at which the physical layer sends a frame's data, set by streams, channel width, modulation, coding rate and guard interval. Application throughput is always lower because of overhead, sharing and retries.
example: Two streams of 64-QAM rate 5/6 on an 80 MHz Wi-Fi 6 channel give a PHY rate of about 720 Mbit/s.

definition: A marketing label on Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) routers giving the sum, in Mbit/s, of the maximum PHY rates of all its radios. No single client can achieve it.
Modulation and coding scheme: an index that names one combination of modulation (e.g. 64-QAM) and coding rate (e.g. 5/6). Higher MCS numbers are faster but need a cleaner signal.
High Efficiency: the 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) name for its physical layer and frame formats.

A short guard period added to every OFDM symbol (in practice a copy of the symbol's end) so echoes of the previous symbol die away before the next is read. Wi-Fi 6 uses 0.8, 1.6 or 3.2 µs; shorter is faster but less tolerant of echoes.
The fraction of transmitted bits that are real data, the rest being error-correction redundancy. A rate of 5/6 means 5 data bits in every 6 sent.
Choosing the MCS (and streams) for each transmission from recent link feedback, dropping to slower, more robust rates when frames fail.
Medium access control: the layer that decides when a device may transmit on a shared medium and frames its data. In Wi-Fi it covers DCF/EDCA contention, ACKs and aggregation.
The fixed training signal sent at the start of every Wi-Fi transmission so the receiver can detect it, synchronise and learn the channel. It costs tens of microseconds per transmission.
MAC protocol data unit: one Wi-Fi MAC frame, header plus payload. Several MPDUs can be aggregated into an A-MPDU.
Aggregated MAC protocol data unit: several MPDUs sent back-to-back in one transmission and acknowledged with one Block Ack, sharing a single channel access.
Sending many frames in one channel access so the fixed cost of contention, PHY preamble and acknowledgement is shared. It is a major reason modern Wi-Fi achieves high efficiency.
example: With a 200 µs fixed cost, one 17 µs frame is 8% efficient; 64 aggregated frames are about 84%.

definition: The fraction of channel time spent sending useful data rather than gaps, backoff, preambles and acknowledgements.
Whether a link can carry traffic in both directions. Full duplex means both at once; half duplex means one direction at a time.
A link on which a device can send or receive but not both at the same moment. A Wi-Fi radio on one channel is half duplex.
A link that carries traffic in both directions at the same time, as switched Ethernet does.
Letting transmissions in different places use the same channel at the same time when they are far enough apart not to interfere. Wi-Fi 6 adds rules to make this more likely.

The 802.11 effect, described by Heusse et al. in 2003, in which one slow station drags down fast ones: DCF gives stations equal chances to send a frame, not equal airtime, so slow frames hog the channel.
example: A 54 Mbit/s client sharing with a 6 Mbit/s client gets only about 5.4 Mbit/s.

definition: Time spent occupying a radio channel. On shared Wi-Fi it is the scarce resource: a slow transmission uses more airtime for the same data.
An access-point scheduling policy that gives clients roughly equal time on air, rather than equal numbers of frames, to stop slow clients starving fast ones.
Variation in received signal strength caused by obstacles, motion and echoes adding or cancelling. It makes radio links change from moment to moment.
Variation in packet delay over time. It hurts calls and games, which need packets to arrive at a steady pace.

Excessive delay caused by oversized buffers that fill up under load, so every packet waits behind a long queue. Ping times jumping from a few to hundreds of milliseconds during a download is the classic sign.
The network layer that moves frames across one link, such as Wi-Fi or Ethernet, using MAC addresses. Wi-Fi retries lost frames at this layer.
The link that carries traffic from an access point or base station back towards the rest of the network.
Received signal strength indicator: a device's measure of how strong an incoming radio signal is, often reported in dBm. Higher (less negative) is stronger.
Signal-to-noise ratio: received signal power divided by noise power, usually in decibels. It sets which modulation a link can use: 1024-QAM needs a very high SNR.
example: A signal 1,000 times stronger than the noise has an SNR of 30 dB.

definition: A logarithmic unit for a ratio of two powers: 10 × log_10(ratio). +3 dB is about double the power, +10 dB ten times, −10 dB a tenth.
Decibels relative to one milliwatt: an absolute power level. 0 dBm is 1 mW, 20 dBm is 100 mW and −70 dBm is a typical decent Wi-Fi signal.
The formula for the highest error-free data rate a noisy channel can carry: C = B × log_2(1 + S/N). Capacity rises in proportion to bandwidth but only logarithmically with signal-to-noise ratio.
example: A 20 MHz channel at 30 dB SNR has a capacity of about 199 Mbit/s.

definition: The power a base must be raised to in order to give a number. log_2(1024) = 10 because 2^10 = 1024; log_10(1000) = 3. Decibels and bits per symbol both use logarithms.
One millionth of a second. Wi-Fi gaps and slots are microseconds long: SIFS is 16 µs.
One thousandth of a second. Network round-trip times are usually given in milliseconds.
One billionth of a second. Light travels about 20 cm in a nanosecond in fibre.
The basic unit of data rate. Network speeds use decimal multiples: kbit/s (10^3), Mbit/s (10^6), Gbit/s (10^9).
One thousand bits per second.
One million bits per second. Home broadband and Wi-Fi rates are usually quoted in Mbit/s.
One billion (10^9) bits per second. Data-centre server ports run at 10–100+ Gbit/s.
10^12 bits per second (1,000 Gbit/s). Fabric totals and submarine cable capacities are quoted in Tbit/s.
10^15 bits per second (1,000 Tbit/s). Google's Jupiter fabric was described as exceeding 1 Pbit/s of bisection bandwidth.
A unit of data of 8 bits. Packet and file sizes are counted in bytes; multiply by 8 to compare with rates in bits per second.
About a thousand bytes: 1,000 in decimal units, though 64 KB TCP window limits are 65,535 bytes.
One million (10^6) bytes in decimal units, as used for network buffer and window sizes in these lessons.
The rate of useful application data delivered, excluding headers, retransmissions and protocol overhead. It is always below the PHY rate.
A wide-area radio network divided into cells, each served by a base station, that lets phones stay connected while moving. 4G (LTE) and 5G are the current generations.
The fourth generation of mobile networks, in practice LTE radio with the EPC core, launched around 2009–2010.
The fifth generation of mobile networks: NR radio plus, in standalone deployments, the 5G core (5GC). Commercial launches began in 2019.
Long Term Evolution: the 3GPP 4G radio technology, using OFDMA downlink and SC-FDMA uplink with centrally scheduled resource blocks.
New Radio: the 3GPP 5G radio interface. It uses OFDM with flexible subcarrier spacing (numerology) across low, mid and millimetre-wave bands.
The 3rd Generation Partnership Project: the body of telecoms standards organisations that writes the LTE and 5G specifications, published in numbered releases.
Access to a mobile core over a network not defined by 3GPP, such as Wi-Fi, through special gateways. Ordinary home Wi-Fi is not connected this way.
User equipment: 3GPP's term for the phone, modem or other device that connects to a mobile network.
Radio access network: the base stations and their links that connect devices over radio to the mobile core.
The central part of a mobile network behind the radio access network. It authenticates subscribers, manages sessions and mobility, and routes user traffic to and from the Internet.
The radio site that serves phones in one or more cells: eNodeB in LTE, gNodeB in 5G NR.
Evolved Node B: the LTE base station. It schedules radio resources and connects to the EPC core.
The 5G NR base station, the counterpart of LTE's eNodeB.
Evolved Packet Core: the LTE core network, with the MME for control and S-GW/P-GW gateways for user traffic.
The 5G core network: a service-based set of functions such as AMF, SMF, UPF, UDM and AUSF. Network slicing is defined here.
Evolved Packet System: LTE radio plus EPC core together.
In LTE, a logical pipe with defined QoS carrying a device's IP traffic between the phone and the P-GW, implemented with GTP tunnels.
Mobility Management Entity: the LTE core's main control node, handling attach, authentication signalling, tracking and handover control.
Access and Mobility Management Function: the 5G core function for registration, connection and mobility management, roughly the MME's successor.
Session Management Function: the 5G core function that sets up and manages PDU sessions, chooses UPFs and allocates device addresses.
Serving Gateway: the LTE user-plane gateway that terminates radio-side tunnels and acts as the local mobility point during handovers between eNodeBs.
PDN Gateway: the LTE gateway to external networks such as the Internet. It anchors the device's IP address for the session.
User Plane Function: the 5G core function that forwards user packets, applies policies and, as session anchor, connects to the Internet.
Home Subscriber Server: the LTE database of subscriber profiles and authentication data.
Unified Data Management: the 5G core function that manages subscriber data and credentials, the HSS's successor role.
Unified Data Repository: the 5G core database that stores subscription and policy data used by UDM and other functions.
Authentication Server Function: the 5G core function that authenticates devices.
The 5G core design in which control-plane functions offer services to each other through HTTP-based APIs, rather than fixed point-to-point protocols.
Version 2 of HTTP, which multiplexes many requests over one connection with binary framing. The 5G core's service-based interfaces use it.
The 5G interface between the SMF and a UPF, over which the SMF installs forwarding rules using the PFCP protocol rather than HTTP.
The part of a network that decides how traffic should be handled: routing protocols, signalling and session set-up. It programs the data plane but does not forward each packet itself.
Mobile-network term for the path that carries users' own packets, as opposed to control signalling. It is the data plane of a mobile network.
The part of a router or switch that forwards each packet: look up the destination, choose an output port, send it, often in hardware at line rate.
The route that ordinary packets actually take through switches and routers (the data plane), as opposed to control-plane exchanges or the path taken by diagnostic replies.
Running a function as software on shared general-purpose hardware instead of on a dedicated box, e.g. mobile-core functions or virtual networks.
In 5G, the association between a device and a data network (such as the Internet) that carries its traffic; PDU means protocol data unit. It can be IP, Ethernet or unstructured.
GPRS Tunnelling Protocol: the mobile-core protocol that carries user packets inside UDP tunnels between base stations and gateways. GTP-U, the user-plane part, uses UDP port 2152.
The gateway (P-GW in LTE, an anchor UPF in 5G) where a device's IP address lives for the session. Handovers move only the radio-side tunnels, so the address seen by the Internet stays the same.
Moving an active connection from one cell or base station to another as a device moves, ideally without dropping the session.
The unit of radio resource an LTE or NR scheduler assigns: 12 subcarriers wide in frequency, for one slot or subframe in time. With 15 kHz spacing it is 180 kHz wide.
The frequency gap between neighbouring OFDM subcarriers: 15 kHz in LTE, 15·2^μ kHz in NR. Wider spacing gives shorter symbols.
A 1 ms unit of the LTE radio frame (ten per 10 ms frame), the conventional LTE scheduling interval.
Transmission time interval: the time unit over which a scheduler assigns one transmission, 1 ms in conventional LTE. Shortened TTIs and NR slots reduce it.
Single-carrier frequency-division multiple access: the LTE uplink waveform, a DFT-spread form of OFDM with lower peak power, which helps phone batteries and amplifiers.
Permission from the base station for a device to transmit on specific resource blocks at a specific time. A connected device asks with a scheduling request; configured grants are pre-arranged.

The procedure a device uses to contact the base station without an existing grant, by sending a short signature sequence on a shared channel. Two devices can collide here, so cellular is not wholly collision-free.
Interference a device or base station receives from transmissions in neighbouring cells using the same frequencies.
In 5G NR, the choice of subcarrier spacing (15·2^μ kHz) and the matching symbol and slot lengths. Higher numerologies give shorter slots for low latency and high bands.
A copy of the end of each OFDM symbol placed in front of it, acting as a guard interval against echoes. 'Normal' cyclic prefix gives 14 symbols per NR slot.
In 5G NR, the scheduling time unit of 14 OFDM symbols (normal cyclic prefix). It lasts 1 ms at 15 kHz spacing and halves with each doubling of spacing.
An NR transmission occupying only a few OFDM symbols instead of a full slot, used for low-latency traffic.

Millimetre wave: strictly 30–300 GHz, but in 5G the term covers the FR2 bands from about 24 GHz upwards. Very wide channels give huge capacity, but the signals are easily blocked by walls, bodies and foliage.
NR Frequency Range 1: the 5G bands below about 7.125 GHz (low and mid bands), carrying most 5G traffic.
NR Frequency Range 2: the 5G millimetre-wave bands, starting at about 24 GHz.
Using an array of antennas to steer radio energy towards a particular device rather than in all directions, extending range and capacity, essential at millimetre-wave frequencies.
An accounting of all gains and losses (transmit power, antennas, path loss, obstacles) between transmitter and receiver, which shows whether enough signal arrives.
Non-standalone 5G: NR radio added alongside an LTE anchor. In the common option 3, LTE and the EPC core handle control, so 5G-core features like slicing are absent.
Standalone 5G: NR radio connected to the 5G core (option 2), without relying on LTE for control.
The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for telecoms. ITU-R sets radio requirements such as IMT-2020 (5G); ITU-T publishes standards such as GPON.
The ITU's requirements for 5G-class systems, including 20 Gbit/s peak downlink and 1 ms URLLC user-plane latency targets under defined test conditions.
Enhanced mobile broadband: the 5G usage scenario for high data rates, such as video on phones. Its IMT-2020 user-plane latency target is 4 ms.
Ultra-reliable low-latency communication: the 5G usage scenario for control traffic such as factory automation, with a 1 ms user-plane latency target.
Radio Resource Control: the LTE/NR protocol between device and base station that sets up and releases radio connections, and so controls the device's power states.
The low-power state in which a device has no RRC connection but still listens for paging. Sending data first needs promotion to RRC_CONNECTED.
The state in which a device has an active radio connection and can be scheduled quickly, at higher power cost.
An NR state between idle and connected: the radio connection is suspended but its context is kept, so resuming is quicker than a full set-up.
How the network tells an idle device that data or a call is waiting: the device wakes periodically to check a paging channel.
An idle device choosing a better cell to camp on as it moves, without a handover because no connection is active.
Discontinuous reception: a device switches its receiver off between scheduled listening windows, saving power at the cost of some delay.
The protocol layers between device and radio network (radio-specific signalling and data transfer), as opposed to the non-access stratum between device and core.
The delay to move a device's radio from idle to connected before data can flow: random access, RRC set-up and security signalling.
Energy a phone's radio spends staying in a high-power state after a transfer ends, until inactivity timers move it to a lower-power state.
A timer that moves the radio to a lower-power state after a period with no data. Its length determines the tail cost of each burst.
The fraction of time something is active. A radio woken for 10 s every 20 s has a 50% duty cycle.
Apple Push Notification service: Apple's platform service that delivers notifications to iOS devices over one shared connection, so apps need not poll.
Firebase Cloud Messaging: Google's push service for delivering messages to Android (and other) apps over one shared connection.
An operating-system service that keeps one shared connection to the platform's servers and wakes apps when a message arrives, replacing per-app polling.
Repeatedly asking a server whether anything has changed, on a timer. On mobile each poll can wake the radio.
A small periodic message sent only to keep a connection or NAT mapping alive, or to detect that it has died.
Carrier-grade NAT: network address translation run by an ISP or mobile operator, so many subscribers share each public IPv4 address.
example: Thousands of phones on one operator can appear to your API as the same IPv4 address.

definition: An entry in a NAT device linking an inside address and port to the public address and port it uses. Mappings expire after idleness.
Interactive Connectivity Establishment: a method for two peers behind NATs to find a working path, by gathering candidate addresses (via STUN and TURN) and testing them.
Session Traversal Utilities for NAT: a protocol that lets a device ask a server what public address and port its NAT gave it. It discovers but does not relay.
Traversal Using Relays around NAT: a relay server that forwards media between peers when no direct path works.
Communication directly between end devices rather than through a central server, as in video calls that use ICE.
The HTTP status code 'Too Many Requests', returned when a client exceeds a rate limit.
An access network that gives devices only IPv6 addresses; IPv4 destinations are reached through translation such as NAT64/DNS64 or 464XLAT.
A translator that lets IPv6-only devices reach IPv4 servers by mapping IPv6 packets to IPv4 and back, usually paired with DNS64.
A DNS resolver that, when a name has only an IPv4 (A) record, synthesises an IPv6 (AAAA) answer pointing at a NAT64 gateway.
An IPv6-transition method (RFC 6877) combining a stateless translator on the device (CLAT) with a stateful NAT64 in the network (PLAT), so IPv4-only apps work on IPv6-only networks.
The client-side translator in 464XLAT: it turns an app's IPv4 packets into IPv6 on the device itself.
An IPv4 address written directly in code or a URL (such as 203.0.113.5) instead of a hostname. It can bypass DNS64 synthesis.
Socket address-family constants: AF_INET means IPv4, AF_INET6 IPv6 and AF_UNSPEC 'either', letting the resolver return whichever families are available.
Creating an IPv6 address that embeds an IPv4 address, as DNS64 and some OS APIs do, so traffic can be sent through NAT64.
The four values that identify a TCP connection: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. The 5-tuple adds the protocol and is what ECMP usually hashes.
In QUIC, an identifier carried in packets that names the connection independently of addresses, so a connection can survive an address change.
QUIC's ability to move an established connection to a new client address or path after validating it.
Multipath TCP: an extension that spreads one TCP connection over several subflows on different paths, e.g. Wi-Fi and cellular, so it can survive losing one.
The iOS/macOS API that reports network path changes and whether the current path is expensive or constrained.
The Android API for querying network state and receiving callbacks when connectivity changes.
Streaming video in several quality levels and switching between them as measured throughput changes.
Hybrid automatic repeat request: fast radio-layer retransmission combined with error correction, which repairs most radio losses within milliseconds before TCP notices.
Radio Link Control: an LTE/NR layer that can retransmit lost data in its acknowledged mode, above HARQ.
Apple's tool for simulating poor networks (added latency, loss, low bandwidth) on a Mac or iPhone; Android emulators have similar network profiles.
Running several logical networks with different capabilities and policies over shared 5G infrastructure, managed by the 5G core.
Multi-access edge computing: placing application servers close to the access network, shortening the path to users.
Refusing new traffic or sessions when accepting them would break guarantees already promised to existing ones.
Subscriber identity module: the card or embedded chip holding a subscriber's identity and the keys used to authenticate to a mobile network.
Radio frequencies an operator has exclusive rights to use (licensed), versus bands anyone may use within rules, such as Wi-Fi's (unlicensed).
The default TCP congestion-control algorithm in Linux and others. Its window grows as a cubic function of time since the last loss and it reacts to loss or ECN marks.

Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time: Google's model-based TCP congestion control, which paces sending from estimates of delivery rate and minimum RTT rather than reacting only to loss.
Explicit Congestion Notification: routers mark packets instead of dropping them when queues build, and the receiver echoes the mark so the sender slows down.
A Linux/Apple socket option that limits how much unsent data the kernel will hold for a socket, reducing local buffering delay for interactive streams.
TCP's start-up phase, in which the congestion window roughly doubles every round trip until loss or a threshold.
First in, first out: a queue that serves packets in arrival order, so a new packet waits for everything ahead of it.
Active queue management: router or AP algorithms (such as CoDel or PIE) that drop or mark packets early to keep queues short and delay low.
A rate-limiting algorithm: tokens accrue at a fixed rate and each packet spends some; when the bucket is empty, packets are dropped or delayed.
Traffic between servers inside a data centre, such as a web server calling a cache or database.
Traffic entering or leaving a data centre, between its servers and the outside world.
The classic hierarchical data-centre design of access (top-of-rack) switches, aggregation switches and core switches. Traffic between branches must climb to the core.
A two-tier data-centre topology in which every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, so any two racks are three switches apart with one equal path per spine.
example: With 8 spines, every pair of leaves has 8 equal-cost paths.

definition: A data-centre network with just two switching layers: leaf switches that servers plug into, and spine switches that connect every leaf. Any two servers on different leaves are one spine apart.
example: With 6 spines, traffic between two racks crosses leaf, spine, leaf: three switches.

definition: In a leaf-spine fabric, the switch servers connect to, usually one (or two) per rack; it has uplinks to every spine.
In a leaf-spine fabric, a switch that connects to every leaf. Spines do not connect to each other; their port count caps the number of leaves.
A third switching tier that connects pods of leaves and spines, extending a Clos fabric beyond one spine layer's port count.
A repeatable block of racks with its own leaf and spine switches, connected to other pods through a super-spine layer.
A multistage switching network, described by Charles Clos in 1953, built from many small switches so it can act like one large non-blocking switch. Leaf-spine is a folded Clos.
A switching network is non-blocking if any idle input can always be connected to any idle output without rearranging existing connections.
The full mesh of switches and links that interconnects a data centre's (or an exchange's) devices and is managed as one system.
A standard frame holding servers and usually a top-of-rack switch; in these lessons one rack is served by one leaf.
The switch at the top of a server rack that the rack's servers plug into; in a leaf-spine fabric it is the leaf.
Spanning Tree Protocol: a layer 2 protocol that prevents loops by blocking redundant links, leaving one active path tree. It wastes the blocked capacity.
The data link layer: forwarding Ethernet frames by MAC address within one network segment (a broadcast domain).
The network layer: forwarding IP packets between networks by destination address, using routing tables.
The transport layer (TCP, UDP). An L4 load balancer chooses a backend using addresses and ports, without reading the application data.
BGP sessions between different autonomous systems. RFC 7938 recommends running eBGP between every leaf and spine in large data centres.
Autonomous system number: the identifier of an autonomous system in BGP, 16 or 32 bits. Data centres often use private ASNs for their switches.
Equal-cost multi-path routing: installing several next hops of equal cost for a destination and spreading traffic across them, usually per flow by hashing headers.
The neighbouring router or switch to which a packet is sent next on its way to the destination.
A sequence of packets that share the same 5-tuple, such as one TCP connection. ECMP keeps each flow on one path to avoid reordering.
The remainder after whole-number division: 14 mod 4 = 2. ECMP often picks path number (hash mod N).
Cyclic redundancy check: a checksum used to detect corrupted data. Ethernet's frame check sequence is a CRC-32; rising CRC errors suggest a bad cable or optic. CRC-32 is also used as a cheap hash.
Two different inputs (here, flows) mapping to the same hash bucket or path. In ECMP, colliding big flows share one link while others sit idle.
A long-lived, high-volume flow, such as a backup or replication stream. A few elephants hashed onto one link can congest it.
Changing a flow's path only after a pause in its packets long enough that packets on the new path cannot overtake earlier ones, balancing load without reordering.
Sending each packet of a flow over a different path to balance load perfectly, which requires a transport that tolerates reordering.
Packets arriving in a different order from the one they were sent in. TCP may mistake reordering for loss and retransmit unnecessarily.
Recomputing which path or server each flow maps to after the set changes, e.g. hash mod 4 becoming hash mod 3; simple modulo rehashing moves most flows.

An ECMP technique that, when a next hop fails, aims to reassign only the flows that were on it and keep other flows on their existing paths. Exact behaviour depends on the implementation's bucket and rebalancing policy.
When switches at successive tiers make correlated hash choices, so some paths get most of the traffic and others little. Different seeds or inputs per tier avoid it.
An extra input mixed into a hash so the same headers give different results on different switches.
Total server-facing bandwidth divided by total uplink bandwidth on a switch (or network). 2:1 means servers could offer twice what the uplinks carry.
example: 48 × 25 Gbit/s down and 6 × 100 Gbit/s up is 1,200 / 600 = 2:1.

definition: The capacity across the narrowest cut that splits a network into two equal halves: the most traffic one half can send the other.
The full nominal speed of a link or port, e.g. 25 Gbit/s.
How much of a system one failure affects. More, smaller spines give each spine failure a smaller blast radius.
A Clos topology built only from identical k-port switches (Al-Fares et al., 2008): k pods supporting k³/4 hosts with full bisection bandwidth in principle.
example: With 48-port switches a fat-tree supports 27,648 hosts.

definition: Google's in-house data-centre network fabric, described in the 2015 paper Jupiter Rising as a Clos topology with over 1 Pbit/s of bisection bandwidth.
Many senders replying to one receiver at the same moment, overflowing the switch buffer on the receiver's port and causing loss, often followed by long retransmission timeouts.
Memory in a switch or router that holds packets waiting for an output port. Shallow buffers drop bursts; deep ones add delay.
A burst of traffic lasting microseconds to milliseconds that briefly exceeds a port's rate, overflowing buffers while averages look low.
How many bytes or packets are waiting in a queue at a given moment.
The fraction of a link's capacity in use, averaged over some interval. Long averages hide short bursts.
Data Center TCP (RFC 8257): a congestion control that estimates the fraction of its bytes that were ECN-marked and cuts its window in proportion, keeping switch queues short.
The sender's limit on unacknowledged data in flight, set by its congestion-control algorithm to avoid overloading the network.
Remote direct memory access: one machine reading or writing another's memory through the network card, bypassing the remote CPU, for very low latency.
RDMA over Converged Ethernet: running RDMA on Ethernet networks. It is sensitive to loss, so deployments often add PFC and congestion notification.
Priority flow control (IEEE 802.1Qbb): a switch tells its neighbour to pause one traffic class when its buffer fills, avoiding drops but risking head-of-line blocking and deadlock.
When the packet at the front of a queue is stuck, everything behind it waits too, even traffic that could have gone elsewhere.
Machine learning. Distributed ML training moves very large flows between servers.
A virtual IP address that represents a service rather than one machine; several load balancers can advertise the same VIP.
Source network address translation: rewriting a packet's source address (and port), e.g. so a load balancer's replies come back to it.
Google's software network load balancer, which uses a consistent-hashing table plus connection tracking so flows stay on the same backend.
A network device that does more than forward packets, such as a firewall, NAT or load balancer, and often keeps per-connection state.
The time needed to put all of a packet's or burst's bits onto a link: size in bits divided by the link rate.
example: 4 MB at 25 Gbit/s takes 1.28 ms to serialise.

definition: The period after a change during which routers exchange updates until they all agree on new routes; packets may be lost meanwhile.
The pluggable module that converts electrical signals to light for a fibre link. Faulty optics cause CRC errors.
Software-defined networking: moving control-plane decisions into software controllers that program switches' forwarding through open interfaces.
The table a data plane looks up for each packet to choose an output port, built from the routing protocols' results.
Open Shortest Path First: a link-state interior routing protocol in which routers share their links and each runs Dijkstra's algorithm to compute shortest paths.
An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from one node to all others in a graph with non-negative link costs; OSPF uses it.
A switch recording which port each source MAC address was seen on, so it can forward later frames to that address out of that port only.
The software that holds the network-wide view in SDN and installs forwarding rules into switches, usually replicated across servers.
Control that behaves as if one brain decides for the whole network, though it may run on several replicated servers.
The interface an SDN controller offers upwards to applications such as traffic engineering or firewalls, often REST.
The interface an SDN controller uses downwards to program switches, e.g. OpenFlow or P4Runtime.
Choosing which paths traffic takes, rather than just the shortest, to use capacity well and meet priorities.
An early, influential SDN protocol (Stanford, around 2008) through which a controller installs match-action entries into switches' flow tables.
A language (2014) for programming how a switch parses packets and processes them in its match-action pipeline, within the hardware's limits; P4Runtime is its control API.
An OpenFlow table of entries, each with match fields, a priority, instructions and counters. The highest-priority matching entry decides what happens to a packet.
The packet header values an OpenFlow entry tests, such as ingress port, MAC and IP addresses, protocol and TCP/UDP ports, possibly with masks.
An OpenFlow entry setting that removes the entry if no packet has matched it for that long.
An OpenFlow entry setting that removes the entry a fixed time after installation, however busy it is.
The lowest-priority (0) catch-all OpenFlow entry that decides what to do with packets no other entry matches: drop, or send to the controller.
An OpenFlow instruction that continues processing a packet in a later flow table of the pipeline.
An OpenFlow message in which a switch sends a packet (or its header) up to the controller, typically on a table miss.
Installing forwarding entries only when a new flow's first packet misses and is sent to the controller. Flexible, but the first packet waits and the controller can be overwhelmed.
Installing forwarding entries in advance from topology and policy, so traffic never waits for the controller.
A forwarding entry that matches many packets by leaving some fields unspecified or masked, e.g. a whole /24, instead of one exact flow.

Ternary content-addressable memory: switch hardware that compares a packet's header with every stored entry at once, with 'don't care' bits, used for wildcard and prefix matching. Fast but small and power-hungry.
Static random-access memory: fast on-chip memory used in switches for exact-match tables and buffers.
An open-source software switch, common in hypervisors, that forwards with OpenFlow-style flow tables.
Network interface card: the hardware connecting a host to a network. A smart NIC can also run tasks such as encapsulation itself.
Google's software-defined WAN connecting its data centres, described in a 2013 paper, with centralised traffic engineering.
Wide area network: a network spanning cities or continents, such as links between data centres.
Operating at the scale of the largest cloud providers, with hundreds of thousands of servers.
Building many isolated logical networks, each with its own addresses and rules, on one shared physical network.
A customer of a shared (cloud) platform whose resources must be isolated from other customers'.
A virtual network built on top of another by encapsulating its packets in packets of the underlying network.
The physical network that carries an overlay's encapsulated packets.
Wrapping a packet inside another protocol's header, as VXLAN or a VPN does, so it can cross a network that only sees the outer header.
The device (hypervisor, switch or NIC) that adds and removes the outer header of a tunnel such as VXLAN.
Virtual Extensible LAN (RFC 7348): carries Ethernet frames inside UDP (port 4789) between tunnel endpoints, with a 24-bit segment ID. It adds 50 bytes over IPv4.
VXLAN Network Identifier: the 24-bit field naming which virtual network a VXLAN packet belongs to, allowing about 16.7 million segments.
Virtual LAN: a layer 2 network separated from others on the same switches by a 12-bit tag, giving 4,094 usable IDs.
Frame check sequence: the 4-byte CRC-32 at the end of an Ethernet frame used to detect corruption.
An Ethernet frame larger than the standard 1,500-byte payload, commonly up to about 9,000 bytes.
Ethernet VPN: using BGP to distribute which MAC and IP addresses are behind which tunnel endpoint, a common control plane for VXLAN.
A virtual private cloud: a logically isolated virtual network in a public cloud (AWS, Google Cloud), with its own address ranges, subnets and routing.
Azure's name for its virtual network, the equivalent of a VPC.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's public cloud platform.
Microsoft's public cloud platform.
Google's public cloud platform.
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud: AWS's virtual machine service; each instance has network interfaces in a VPC subnet.
An isolated group of data centres within a cloud region with independent power and networking. An AWS subnet lives in one zone.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing notation: an address range written as address/prefix length, e.g. 10.20.0.0/16, where the prefix length counts the fixed leading bits.
example: A /20 leaves 12 host bits: 2^12 = 4,096 addresses.

definition: The number after the slash in CIDR notation: how many leading bits are fixed. Longer prefixes are smaller, more specific ranges.
A contiguous block of IP addresses carved out of a larger range; in AWS, a subnet sits in one availability zone.
A list of destination ranges and where to send matching traffic (next hop or gateway).
The AWS VPC component that connects public subnets to the Internet when a route points at it.
An AWS stateful, allow-only virtual firewall attached to instances' network interfaces. Replies to allowed traffic are permitted automatically.
Network access control list: an AWS stateless firewall attached to a subnet, with numbered allow and deny rules evaluated in order, first match wins.
Access control list: an ordered list of rules saying which traffic is permitted or denied.
Remembering earlier packets, e.g. connection state, so later packets (such as replies) are handled in context.
Judging each packet on its own, with no memory of earlier packets; a stateless filter needs explicit rules for replies.
A temporary source port the OS picks for an outgoing connection; replies return to it. Linux uses 32768–60999 by default (28,232 ports).
An address valid only on the local link (169.254.0.0/16 in IPv4, fe80::/10 in IPv6); AWS exposes some services at link-local addresses.
Bring your own IP: moving address ranges you own into a cloud provider so your resources keep them.
A private routed connection between two VPCs. It is not transitive and needs non-overlapping address ranges plus routes on both sides.
A relationship that carries through: if A connects to B and B to C, then A connects to C. VPC peering is not transitive.
An AWS regional hub router that many VPCs and VPNs attach to, with its own route tables, replacing a full mesh of peerings.
An AWS service that exposes one service from a VPC as an interface endpoint inside another, without routing between the two networks.
A network interface in your subnet, created by PrivateLink, that reaches a specific service in another VPC or AWS.
Infrastructure in an organisation's own buildings or data centres rather than in a public cloud.
Changing the IP addresses used by a network, which touches every device, rule and dependency.
A consistent network update: install new rules tagged with a new version, switch ingress to stamp the new tag, then remove old rules after in-flight packets drain.
A place where packets are silently discarded, e.g. a switch with no matching rule, without informing the sender.
An AWS feature that records accepted and rejected IP traffic for VPC network interfaces, used for debugging and auditing.
A cloud tool that checks, from configuration, whether traffic could pass between two resources and which rule blocks it.
OpenFlow switch behaviours on losing the controller: fail-secure keeps using installed entries (dropping misses); fail-standalone falls back to acting as a normal learning switch.
An OpenFlow group that forwards via the first live port in its list, switching to a backup locally when a link fails, without the controller.
An OpenFlow request whose reply confirms the switch has finished processing all earlier messages, used to sequence rule updates.
A single hardened server that administrators log in to first, the only one exposed for SSH, before reaching private machines.
An AWS service for opening shell sessions on instances through the AWS API, without opening inbound SSH ports.
Point-to-Point Protocol over Ethernet, used by many DSL connections. Its 8-byte header reduces the MTU to 1,492 bytes.
The IP forwarding rule: of all routes containing the destination address, use the one with the longest (most specific) prefix.
example: For 192.0.2.10, a /24 route beats a covering /22.

definition: An IPv4 header option in which routers write their addresses into the packet; it holds only nine addresses and is widely ignored.

Internet Control Message Protocol: the IP companion protocol for error and diagnostic messages, such as echo request/reply (ping), Time Exceeded (traceroute) and Destination Unreachable. ICMPv6 is the IPv6 version.
The ICMP error a router sends back when it discards a packet whose TTL (hop limit) reached zero. Traceroute relies on it to reveal each hop.
The ICMP error a host returns when a UDP packet arrives for a port nobody is listening on; it tells traceroute it has reached the destination.
The ICMPv6 error a router sends when a packet is larger than the next link's MTU; IPv6 routers never fragment, so senders depend on it for PMTUD.
The IPv4 ICMP error (type 3, code 4) a router sends when a packet with DF set is too big for the next link, carrying that link's MTU.
The IPv4 Don't Fragment flag. A router must drop an oversized DF packet and return 'fragmentation needed' instead of splitting it.
Splitting an IP packet that is too big for a link into smaller pieces, reassembled at the destination.
Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest MTU on a path by sending packets that must not be fragmented and listening for ICMP 'too big' errors.
A path where large packets are silently dropped because the ICMP 'too big' messages that would tell the sender to shrink them are blocked. Small requests work; large transfers hang.
Finding the path MTU by probing with progressively larger packets at the transport layer and watching which are acknowledged, without relying on ICMP.
Maximum segment size: the largest TCP payload one segment may carry, typically 1,460 bytes on a 1,500-byte MTU (1,500 − 20 IP − 20 TCP).
A router rewriting the MSS option in TCP SYN packets to a smaller value so connections through a tunnel never send packets too big for it.
Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel carrying private traffic across another network. The added headers reduce the MTU available inside.
Carrying one network's packets inside another network's packets (encapsulation), as VPNs, VXLAN and GTP do.
Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for remote login and commands, on TCP port 22.
A tool that sends ICMP echo requests and reports whether replies arrive and their round-trip times.
A tool that reveals the routers on a path by sending probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 … and reading the ICMP Time Exceeded replies.
A tool that runs traceroute continuously and shows per-hop loss and latency statistics.
A command-line DNS lookup tool that shows the full answer, including TTLs; +trace follows delegation from the root.
A command-line tool for making HTTP and other requests; -w prints timing milestones such as time_connect and time_starttransfer.
The Linux socket statistics tool, the modern replacement for netstat; -i shows TCP internals such as rtt, cwnd and retransmissions.
An older tool for listing sockets and network statistics, largely replaced by ss on Linux.
A packet-capture tool that records and prints packets matching a filter, saving them to pcap files for analysis.
A small tool (nc) for opening TCP or UDP connections by hand, useful to test whether a port connects.
An OpenSSL command that opens a TLS connection and prints the handshake and certificates, for testing TLS.
In Linux ping output, the standard deviation of the round-trip times: how much they spread around the average. High mdev means variable delay.
In ss output for an established TCP socket, bytes the application has written that the peer has not yet acknowledged (Send-Q) or that the application has not yet read (Recv-Q).
Sending data again because it was (or appears to have been) lost.
A retransmission of data that was not actually lost, e.g. triggered by reordering or a timer firing too early.
A TCP ACK repeating the same acknowledgement number because a later segment arrived out of order; three in a row trigger fast retransmit.
TCP's way of repairing a loss signalled by duplicate ACKs: retransmit the missing segment and keep sending, rather than waiting for a timeout.
Retransmission timeout: how long TCP waits for an acknowledgement before resending. Linux's default minimum is 200 ms, so a timeout stall is long compared with data-centre RTTs.
RACK (Recent ACKnowledgment) detects TCP losses by time rather than counts, and TLP (tail loss probe) resends the last segment early, so lost tails need not wait for an RTO (RFC 8985).
The first TCP packet of a connection, carrying the SYN (synchronise) flag; the client's opening move in the three-way handshake.
The server's reply to a SYN, carrying both SYN and ACK flags; the second step of the TCP handshake.
A TCP segment with the reset flag, which aborts a connection or refuses one, e.g. when nothing is listening on the port.
The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection, costing about one round trip before data can flow.
The exchange that sets up a TLS session: agree versions and keys and verify certificates. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip; TLS 1.2 typically two.
The server's certificate plus the intermediate certificates linking it to a trusted root; a long chain makes the TLS handshake bigger.
Time to first byte: from the start of a request until the first response byte arrives. In curl it is cumulative, including DNS, connect and TLS.
An algorithm (RFC 8305) that tries IPv6 and IPv4 connections in a staggered race and uses whichever succeeds first.
Version 3 of HTTP, running over QUIC (UDP) instead of TCP.
Carrying several streams of data over one link or connection at once.
An intermediary that forwards requests on behalf of clients, adding its own connections and delay.
The server that looks up names for clients, following referrals and caching answers for their TTL.
Giving different DNS answers for the same name depending on who asks, e.g. private addresses inside a company and public ones outside.
DNS Security Extensions: digital signatures on DNS records that let resolvers verify answers have not been tampered with.
A DNS server that holds the actual records for a zone and answers for it, rather than from a cache.
A DNS record mapping a name to an IPv6 address (an A record maps to IPv4).
A resolver policy (RFC 8767) of answering from expired cache entries when the authoritative servers cannot be reached.
A local file mapping names to addresses that the OS checks before (or instead of) DNS.
A suffix the resolver appends to short names, so 'app' may be looked up as 'app.corp.example'.
The OS object an application uses to send and receive over the network, identified for TCP by local and remote address and port.
A TCP socket waiting for incoming connections on a port. With none, the host replies to a SYN with RST: 'connection refused'.
The error when a connection attempt is actively rejected, usually by a TCP RST because nothing is listening on that port, or by a firewall reject rule.
Giving up on an operation after a deadline passes without an answer. A connection timeout usually means packets were silently dropped somewhere.
The amount of data a TCP receiver says it can accept, advertised in each ACK. A zero window tells the sender to stop until the application reads data.
Mechanisms that stop a sender overwhelming a receiver; in TCP, the advertised receive window.
A tiny segment a TCP sender sends periodically while the receiver's window is zero, to learn when it reopens.
A TCP option that multiplies the 16-bit window field so windows can exceed 64 KB, needed for fast long-distance paths.
Link rate multiplied by round-trip time: the amount of data that must be in flight to keep a path full.
example: 1 Gbit/s × 100 ms = 100 Mbit = 12.5 MB.

definition: A 1997 formula (Mathis et al.) for steady-state TCP Reno throughput with periodic loss: about (MSS/RTT) × 1.22/√p. Throughput falls with the square root of the loss rate.
A classic TCP congestion control: grow the window by one segment per round trip, halve it on loss (with fast recovery).
The TCP phase after slow start in which the window grows slowly (about one segment per round trip for Reno) to probe for capacity.
The Linux kernel's table of active connections, used by stateful firewalls and NAT. When it fills, new connections fail.
The TCP state the side that closes first stays in for a while (60 s on Linux) so stray old packets cannot confuse a new connection with the same 4-tuple; the port stays tied up.
Running out of free source ports for new connections to one destination, often because many recently closed sockets sit in TIME_WAIT.
A firewall that tracks connections and allows replies automatically, but drops packets of connections it never saw, e.g. with asymmetric routing.
Requests and replies taking different paths, which traceroute cannot show and which can break stateful firewalls.
Request for Comments: the numbered document series that publishes Internet standards and best practices, e.g. RFC 7348 for VXLAN.
The open-source operating-system kernel used by most servers; its networking defaults are referred to throughout these lessons.
The standard file format for captured packets, written by tcpdump and read by Wireshark.
Letting the network card do work such as checksums or splitting large segments, so a capture on the host may show packets that differ from those on the wire.
A network or group of networks under one administration with one routing policy, identified by an AS number and connected to others with BGP.
The BGP attribute listing the autonomous systems a route announcement has passed through. Shorter is preferred after policy, but it says nothing about distance or speed.
Adding your own AS number to an announcement several times to make the path look longer and so less attractive.
A paid service in which a provider carries a customer's traffic to and from the whole Internet.
Two networks exchanging traffic directly between themselves and their customers only, not to the rest of the Internet.
Peering in which neither side pays the other for exchanged traffic, though each still pays for its ports and circuits.
A network that can reach every Internet destination through its own customers and settlement-free peering, without buying transit.
A network that peers widely but still buys transit for some destinations.
A network that mainly buys transit and does little peering; a stub network has only providers, no customers.
The pattern produced by commercial export rules: a path goes up through providers, crosses at most one peering link, then goes down through customers.
A network announcing routes beyond their intended scope, e.g. passing one provider's routes to another, so traffic is drawn through it.
Announcing IP prefixes you do not own (often more specific ones) so traffic for them is drawn to you.
Resource Public Key Infrastructure: certificates proving who holds IP address blocks and AS numbers, used to sign ROAs.
Checking that a BGP announcement's origin AS and prefix length are authorised by a valid ROA, and marking it Valid, Invalid or NotFound. It does not check the rest of the path.
Route Origin Authorisation: a signed RPKI object stating which AS may originate a prefix, up to what maximum length.
A list of which prefixes a network will accept from a neighbour, e.g. only those its customer actually holds.
Netflix's content delivery network, which places caching servers inside ISPs' networks and at exchange points.
Google's caching servers placed inside ISPs' networks to serve YouTube and other content locally.
Internet service provider: a company that sells Internet access to homes and businesses.
Internet exchange point: a shared switching fabric, usually across colocation sites in one city, where many networks connect and exchange traffic by peering.
A data centre that rents space, power and connectivity to many organisations, where networks can meet and cross-connect.
A server at an IXP that collects routes from members over BGP and redistributes them, so one session reaches many peers. Data still flows directly between members.
Private network interconnect: a dedicated link between two networks, rather than via a shared IXP fabric, used for large traffic volumes.
A physical cable run inside a colocation facility connecting two customers' equipment directly.
A large Internet exchange operator, headquartered in Frankfurt.
The Amsterdam Internet Exchange, one of the largest exchange points.
The London Internet Exchange, the UK's largest exchange point.
A fibre-optic cable laid on the seabed between countries or continents. They carry most intercontinental Internet traffic.
Two optical fibres, one per direction, forming one bidirectional path in a cable.
Dense wavelength-division multiplexing: sending many independent signals on different light colours down one fibre, multiplying its capacity.
A device that boosts light in a fibre without converting it to electricity; long submarine cables have amplifiers (repeaters) every several tens of kilometres, powered from shore.
Direct current at thousands of volts sent along a submarine cable's conductor from landing stations to power its repeaters.
A Google-owned transatlantic cable between the US and France, ready for service in 2021, announced at 250 Tbit/s.
The International Cable Protection Committee, an industry body that publishes guidance and statistics on submarine cable faults.
The final link from an ISP to a home or business (DSL, cable, fibre or radio), often the bottleneck.
Digital subscriber line: broadband over the telephone copper pair. Rates fall as the line gets longer.
Asymmetric DSL: an older DSL with much faster download than upload.
Very-high-bit-rate DSL 2: faster DSL for short copper runs, typically from a street cabinet.

aliases: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification
definition: Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification: the standard for broadband over cable-TV coaxial networks, where a neighbourhood shares capacity.
Cable with a central conductor inside a shield, used by cable-TV and DOCSIS broadband.
Passive optical network: one fibre from the exchange split by unpowered splitters to many homes, which share its capacity.
Gigabit-capable PON (ITU-T G.984): 2.48832 Gbit/s down and 1.24416 Gbit/s up, shared by all homes on the split.
10-gigabit-symmetric PON (ITU-T G.9807.1): about 9.95 Gbit/s each way, shared by the split.
Fibre to the premises: optical fibre all the way to the building, usually delivered as a PON.
Optical line terminal: the PON equipment at the exchange that sends the shared downstream signal and schedules upstream turns.
Optical network terminal: the PON box in the customer's premises; it receives the shared stream and keeps only its own traffic.
An unpowered device that divides one fibre's light among several fibres, e.g. 1:32, so many homes share one PON.
Broadband to a building over a radio link (4G/5G or other) instead of a cable.
Users competing for a shared resource: stations for airtime on a Wi-Fi channel, or subscribers for an ISP's shared capacity.
The hour of the day with the highest traffic, which networks are dimensioned for.
How much slower light travels in a material than in a vacuum. Fibre glass is about 1.47, so light there travels at about 204,000 km/s.
About 299,792 km/s in a vacuum; slower in glass. It sets the minimum possible delay of any long-distance link.
The time a signal takes to travel the physical distance: distance divided by signal speed, about 5 µs per km of fibre.
Time a packet spends waiting in a buffer behind other packets before it can be sent.
Geostationary orbit: about 35,786 km above the equator, where a satellite circles once a day and so appears fixed in the sky. Round trips via GEO take at least about 477 ms.
Low Earth orbit, roughly 160–2,000 km up. Satellites there move across the sky but give round trips of only milliseconds, so services need many of them.
A group of satellites working together to cover the Earth; LEO services need many because each sees only a small area.
A satellite that simply relays signals from the user down to a nearby ground station, without routing between satellites.
The actual line-of-sight distance from a ground station to a satellite that is not directly overhead, always longer than the altitude.
A site with large antennas that links satellite traffic to the terrestrial Internet.
A direct link between satellites, often by laser, so traffic can cross space in vacuum without landing.
An antenna made of many elements whose timing is adjusted to steer the beam electronically, letting a dish-less terminal track moving satellites.
One thousand metres. Light covers about 204 km per millisecond in fibre and 300 km in a vacuum.
A device that forwards IP packets between networks using its routing table.
The mobile-core node that carries user traffic between the radio network and the Internet: S-GW and P-GW in LTE, UPF in 5G. Its control logic sets up the tunnels for each session.
A managed device or cloud service that performs NAT for many hosts' outbound connections; it has its own limits on concurrent connections and ports.
A server in front of backend services that receives client API calls and forwards them, often opening many outbound connections itself.
The buffer in front of a switch or router's outgoing port where packets wait to be sent; when it is full, new arrivals are dropped (output drops).
A 4-byte field placed before each MPDU inside an A-MPDU, giving its length and a check value so the receiver can find frame boundaries.
The part of an ISP's network that collects traffic from many access lines (exchanges, cabinets, PON OLTs) and carries it to the core; usually oversubscribed.
The Internet Protocol: the network-layer protocol that carries packets between networks using IP addresses. IPv4 and IPv6 are its two versions.
Operating system: the software, such as Linux, iOS or Android, that manages a device's hardware and provides networking to apps.
A table of how much traffic each source sends to each destination; a network's performance depends on which matrix it faces.
One request triggering many parallel requests to other services or shards, whose replies then converge on the requester.
Connecting a server to two switches instead of one, for redundancy.
Steering traffic through a sequence of network functions such as a firewall then a load balancer, which can lengthen its path.
Apple's development environment for iOS and macOS apps; its additional tools include the Network Link Conditioner.
